why_this_tool: Temporal makes every agent step a recorded event that is replayed after a crash, so orchestration patterns, retries, checkpoints and human approval can all be practised on one laptop with a single engine.
alternatives: LangGraph checkpoints graph state inside the agent framework itself, AWS Step Functions runs declarative state machines as a managed cloud service, the OpenAI Agents SDK and the Claude Agent SDK coordinate agent handoffs and tools but leave durability to you, and plain Postgres can hold hand-rolled checkpoints with no replay engine.

setup.do: Read what durable execution means and which failures it is meant to absorb before installing anything.
setup.done_when: You can state in one sentence what happens to a running workflow when its worker process dies.
setup.why: Every later step tests one claim: a run survives crashes without losing or repeating work. Knowing the claim first tells you what to look for.

setup.do: Pick the SDK language you know best and install that SDK and the Temporal command line tool by following its quickstart.
setup.done_when: The Temporal command line tool prints its version and the SDK imports cleanly in an empty project.
setup.why: The quickstart installs a local development service, the web UI and the SDK together, with no paid cloud and no GPU.

setup.do: Learn the parts of a Temporal application: workflows, activities, workers and the client that starts runs.
setup.done_when: You can sketch your planned agent on paper with each box labelled workflow, activity, worker or client.
setup.why: Agent code splits along these lines: deterministic orchestration goes in the workflow, model and tool calls go in activities.

setup.do: Start the local development service and open its web UI in a browser.
setup.done_when: The web UI loads and shows an empty list of workflow executions in the default namespace.
setup.why: The server holds all run state, so nothing executes until it is up, and the UI is where you will read event histories.

steps.do: Run the quickstart workflow for your SDK from start to finish against the local service.
steps.done_when: The web UI shows one workflow execution with status Completed and a result value.
steps.why: A first complete run proves the worker, the client and the server are talking before you add any agent logic.

steps.do: Write a workflow that models one agent loop: an activity that calls a stubbed model, then an activity that calls a stubbed tool, repeated until the stub says done.
steps.done_when: A run completes and its event history lists one scheduled and one completed event per model call and tool call.
steps.why: This is the core object model for agents: the workflow decides which step runs next and what context it gets, while activities do the unreliable work.

steps.do: Run the agent workflow with a slow tool activity, kill the worker process halfway through, then start the worker again.
steps.done_when: The run finishes after the restart and the already completed model calls appear only once in the history.
steps.why: This is the durability promise tested directly: a long run must continue from where it stopped instead of restarting from the top.

steps.do: Compare the event history of the resumed run with your workflow code, line by line, to trace how replay rebuilt its state.
steps.done_when: You can point at each history event and name the line of workflow code that produced it.
steps.why: Replay is how a workflow engine restores state without a snapshot. Understanding it explains every rule about what workflow code may do.

steps.do: Create a deliberate non-deterministic change by reordering two activity calls in the workflow while a run is still open, then restart the worker.
steps.done_when: The open run reports a non-determinism error in the worker log or web UI, and it recovers when you revert the change.

verified.section_found: Code changes can cause non-deterministic behavior

steps.why: Deploys happen while agent runs are in flight, and a changed workflow that no longer matches its history fails on replay.

steps.do: Write an orchestrator workflow that fans work out to three specialist agent workflows in parallel and merges their results.
steps.done_when: The web UI shows one parent execution linked to three child executions, and the parent result contains all three outputs.
steps.why: Fan-out and fan-in with a supervisor is the most common multi-agent coordination pattern, and the task orchestration patterns show how to express it durably.

steps.do: Create a second coordination variant from the AI agent design patterns, such as a router that hands off to one specialist agent chosen by the model output.
steps.done_when: Two runs with different inputs each start a different specialist, visible as different child executions in the UI.
steps.why: Comparing a handoff pattern with the fan-out pattern on the same engine shows which context each agent receives and what each pattern costs.

steps.do: Configure a retry policy with backoff and a maximum attempt count on the model activity, make the stub fail with a rate limit error twice, and pass an idempotency key to the tool activity.
steps.done_when: The history shows the model activity succeeding on its third attempt and the tool stub logs exactly one side effect per key.
steps.why: Retries make rate limits survivable, but a retried tool call that is not idempotent repeats side effects such as sending a message twice.

steps.do: Enable a budget guard that tracks steps and estimated token spend in workflow state and requests cancellation when the cap is exceeded, with cleanup in the activities.
steps.done_when: A run with a low cap ends with status Canceled, and the cleanup step appears in its history.
steps.why: An agent loop without a ceiling can burn money indefinitely. Cancellation stops it cleanly while still letting in-flight work clean up.

steps.do: Write a human approval gate: the workflow waits before a risky tool call until an approve or reject message arrives, and a read-only message returns the pending action.
steps.done_when: A run sits in Running until you send approval from the command line tool, then completes, and a rejection takes the other branch.

steps.why: The wait is a durable checkpoint that can last days at no compute cost. Choosing the right message type decides whether the approver gets a confirmed result.

steps.do: Compare the persisted event histories of a clean run and a crashed and resumed run of the same agent, then restart the local service with a database file and check that both are still there.
steps.done_when: Both histories show the same sequence of completed activities, and both runs are still listed after a full service restart.
steps.why: The persistence layer is where checkpoints actually live. Comparing two histories is how you prove no step was lost or repeated.

steps.do: Deploy a self-hosted Temporal Service in containers with Postgres as the persistence store, point your workers at it, and rerun the approval and crash tests; this is the local substitute for the paid managed cloud.
steps.done_when: The agent workflow survives a restart of the worker container and of the server container, and its history is readable from the Postgres-backed service.

steps.why: Production separates the server, the database and the workers, so repeating the tests against that shape shows what you would operate for real.
